newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria on fresh bomb alert ahead of elections.
newsitem.headline: Austria on fresh bomb alert ahead of elections.

text.p: The Austrian government on Tuesday sounded a fresh warning of possible bomb attacks in a suspected right-wing extremist campaign that has confounded security services for three years.
The alert came in the midst of campaigning for European parliamentary elections and a Vienna state poll on October 13.
An interior ministry spokesman said a group calling itself the Bajuvarian Liberation Army had written to current affairs magazine Profil warning of eight bombs.

Police chiefs later confirmed that the note bore the same hallmarks as messages attached by the group to letter bombs that have either exploded or been intercepted by police since the campaign began in December 1993.
"The government is taking this warning very seriously and supports the interior ministry in any action it needs to take," Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told reporters.
In a worrying development, the warning sent to Profil spoke for the first time only of bombs.
"The fact that this message makes no specific reference to letter bombs, means that other attacks cannot be ruled out," Interior Minister Caspar Einem said in a statement.
Police suspect neo-Nazis are behind the campaign. Government sources have indicated that the Bajuvarian Liberation Army may consist of a group of middle-aged fanatics.
They are believed to be obsessed with reuniting German-speaking peoples in Bavaria, the Alps and the Danube River -- a distinct region which existed between the sixth and 12th centuries.
The group has claimed responsibility for more than 20 letter bombs directed against foreigners and figures linked to immigrant or refugee issues since 1993.
Most have exploded, injuring 11 people, including former Vienna mayor, Helmut Zilk.

Four gypsy men died last year when a booby-trapped bomb exploded as they tried to remove a racist sign. In 1994, a pipe bomb, planted outside a Slovenian language school in southern Austria, exploded, mangling the hands of a police officer.
The letter bomb attacks spilled over into Germany last year when German television personality Arabella Kiesbauer, whose father is Ghanaian, suffered facial injuries in a blast.
Former Slovenian foreign minister Lojze Peterle received a threat in a letter posted from Austria in 1994.

Einem said the eight people threatened in the latest warning were well-known public figures, not only in Austria but also outside the country. All have been contacted but no names, or the countries involved, have been released to the media.
"The way this letter looks and the way it is written leads us to believe it is authentic," Robert Sturm, chief of the interior ministry bomb investigation unit, told Austrian radio.
Sturm said the letter had been posted in the town of Weisskirchen in the southern Austrian province of Styria.

Despite questioning around 50,000 people and poring over 400,000 pages of related reports, police remain baffled by the bombings, drawing widespread public criticism of the state's security apparatus.
The only arrests have been of two young neo-Nazis who were acquitted in December 1995. No one has been charged with the murders of the four gypsies.
